findings.cause:
The driver is `WorkspaceSyncService.synchronizeVectorStore` (WorkspaceSyncService.swift:2316), not `mergeVectorStoresIfNeeded`. The call path is exact and the log signature matches it line for line.

THE UNIT (4 loads, 2 buffers, 2 persists per synced container per pass)
`synchronizeVectorStore` does, for one container with one source id:
  1. :2340 `loadVectorChunks(local)`  -> constructs a BNNSVectorDatabase (:1876) -> `init` spawns `loadFromDisk` (BNNSVectorDatabase.swift:96) -> one `[BNNS] Loaded N`.
  2. :2368 `loadVectorChunks(shared)` -> second construction -> second `Loaded N`.
  3. :2445 `persistVectorChunks(-> localVectorURL)` -> third construction (:2461) -> third `Loaded N`, then `clear()`, `storeBatch` -> `Batch buffered N`, `persist()` -> `Persisted N`.
  4. :2446 `persistVectorChunks(-> sharedVectorURL)` -> fourth construction -> fourth `Loaded N`, `Batch buffered N`, `Persisted N`.
That is literally `L L L B P L B P`, and that is exactly the repeating unit in the capture (Startup.txt:48-55, 56-63, and every burst after). `mergeVectorStoresIfNeeded` would emit `L L L B P` (3 opens, 1 write) and never appears. Ruled out.

THE PERIODICITY
A "20-load burst" is one `synchronizeConfiguredLibraries` pass over 5 synced containers holding 26 / 182 / 182 / 182 / 1451 chunks (4 loads each). After a library is deleted mid-session (Startup.txt:878-887) bursts drop to 16 loads = 4 containers. The arithmetic closes: 250+88+91 = 429 of the 432 loads, and 122+44+44 = 210 persists exactly, i.e. ~21 full passes in one boot. The residual 3 loads are single `L0`/`L26`/`L182` lines from `VectorStoreRouter` re-opens.

A "40-load burst" is not two refreshes. It is two byte-identical 20-load passes back to back with zero interleaving and one queue restore after (Startup.txt:212-291, 366-447, 456-535). That is the coalescing `repeat { ... } while needsReconfigurePass` in `reconfigureIfNeeded` (WorkspaceSyncService.swift:352 sets the flag, :369 loops): a second trigger arriving during a pass returns early and makes the in-flight call run the whole pass again. Bursts are therefore always exact multiples of one pass.

The brief's framing has the causality backwards on one point: `restorePersistedIngestionQueueIfNeeded` (RAGService.swift:1045) does NOT open any vector store - it deliberately reads `Document.totalChunks` instead (comment at RAGService.swift:1108-1118). The `Dropping persisted ingestion item` lines are the TAIL of a refresh cycle, emitted by `reloadWorkspaceData()` (RAGService.swift:3675, spawned at :3684), not its cause. "40 loads per queue restore" is really "one refresh cycle = N passes then one queue restore".

WHY IT REPEATS ~21 TIMES (the loop)
User actions cannot account for it: the whole session contains 1 tab change, 6 `Scene became inactive`, 4 `Container changed`. The pass re-triggers itself, through two independent code-provable channels, both of which write into the very directory the sync's own trigger watches:
  (a) Every pass unconditionally rewrites the SHARED `containers.json` (:1262) and `documents_metadata.json` (:1297) via `coordinatedMergeData`, which always calls `merged.write(to:options:.atomic)` (:3461) with no byte comparison. `isWorkspaceMetadataItemRelevant` (:3292) filters out only names beginning `vector_database_`, so both of those files are relevant, and `workspaceSignature` (:3299) hashes `NSMetadataItemFSContentChangeDateKey` - so an identical-bytes rewrite still changes the signature. `handleMetadataQueryResults` (:3252) then does `observedWorkspaceChangeCount += 1` (:3273), which ContentView.swift:237 turns into `refreshSharedWorkspaceIfNeeded(forceReload: true)` -> :382 `reconfigureIfNeeded()` -> another full pass. There is no `isSyncWriteInProgress` guard on that handler and no debounce beyond the query's 0.75s batching.
  (b) `synchronizeAuxiliaryFile` (:2470) picks the newest of `transcript_*` / `chat_history_*` / `conversation_memory_*` by `max(by: modificationDate)` (:2492) and copies it across via `coordinatedCopyItem` (:3506), which removes and re-copies the destination and therefore always leaves the DESTINATION newer than the source. Next pass the roles flip and it copies back. This is a guaranteed alternating rewrite of a watched file in each root on every single pass, with no external cause at all.

THE COST (this is real work, not just frequency)
The FileProvider errors quantify it. Their sizes are exact arithmetic matches for the vector artifacts, five of them independently: `sz:104 bytes` = 26x4 (26-chunk `_norms.bin`, Startup.txt:162), `sz:728 bytes` = 182x4 (:153), `sz:6 KB` = 1451x4 (:148), `sz:40 KB` = 26x384x4 = 39,936 (:141), `sz:280 KB` = 182x384x4 = 279,552 (:149). The `_meta.json` files show as `sz:531 KB` (182-chunk, :143) and `sz:59 KB` (26-chunk). Every one carries `(replacing:...)` and `ul:uploading(?%)`. So each persist deletes and rewrites three real files, and half of them go into the iCloud ubiquity container as replacement uploads.
Per pass, per destination: 26-store ~99 KB + three 182-stores ~812 KB each + the 1451-store (2.2 MB vectors measured from the `mmap'd 2MB` log line, 6 KB norms, plus a `_meta.json` extrapolated at the measured 2.9 KB/chunk to ~4.2 MB). Two destinations. That is a measured floor of ~9 MB per pass and a likely ~18 MB, times ~21 passes: at minimum ~200 MB written per boot, roughly half of it queued to iCloud, for zero content change.
Also gratuitous: `loadVectorChunks` calls `getEmbeddings(forIndices:)` (BNNSVectorDatabase.swift:750), which allocates one `[Float]` per chunk and copies every vector out of the mmap onto the heap - 1451 allocations and 2.2 MB for the big store, twice per pass - which is precisely what the mmap design exists to avoid.

MAIN ACTOR
Mostly no. `BNNSVectorDatabase` is an actor; `loadFromDisk` (:143) and `saveToDisk` (:291) run on its executor, and `init` only spawns the load Task (:96). The four constructions are wrapped in `await MainActor.run { }` (WorkspaceSyncService.swift:1857, :1876, :2461), so the session performs 432 main-thread hops, but each hop stores three fields and creates a Task. `WorkspaceSyncService` is `@MainActor` (:213) yet every heavy helper is `nonisolated async`, so it runs off-main. The 2.94s hang is logged at Startup.txt:47, one line BEFORE the first `[BNNS] Loaded` at :48 and right after `NSMapGet ... is NULL` at :46 - this log does not attribute the hang to the churn, and I am not claiming it does.

Sibling lines give 728 B (:153, 182x4), 6 KB (:148, 1451x4), 40 KB (:141, 26x1536), 280 KB (:149, 182x1536), 531 KB _meta.json (:143). Five exact arithmetic matches - the persists write real bytes and re-upload them.

findings.fix:
Four changes, cheapest first. The first alone removes both persists and half the loads.

1. Short-circuit the no-op write in `synchronizeVectorStore` (WorkspaceSyncService.swift:2445-2446). `mergeVectorChunks` (:1923-1929) returns a deterministic order (sorted by documentId then chunkIndex), and `localChunks` / `sharedChunks` are already in hand from :2340 and :2368. Build a cheap digest (count + ordered chunk ids) of `resolvedChunks` and of each destination's already-loaded list, and skip that destination's `persistVectorChunks` when they match. No extra I/O. Effect: 210 persists -> ~0 on an idle boot, 432 loads -> ~216, and all vector-artifact iCloud re-uploads stop.

2. Stop the pass re-triggering itself. Both channels need closing:
   a. `handleMetadataQueryResults` (:3252) must not treat this app's own sync writes as a remote change. Have the pass record the set of shared-root paths it wrote and have the handler exclude those paths from the signature comparison until their content dates settle. A blanket `isSyncWriteInProgress` mute is not enough - the notification arrives after the pass ends (0.75s batching plus iCloud latency).
   b. `synchronizeAuxiliaryFile` (:2470) must compare source and destination bytes before copying and skip when equal, so `coordinatedCopyItem` stops flipping which side is "newest" on every pass.

3. Make `coordinatedMergeData` (:3445) skip the write when the transform returns bytes identical to what it just read. This is a one-line guard that removes the containers.json / documents_metadata.json content-date churn feeding 2(a), and it also cuts the sync's iCloud upload traffic independently of the vector work.

4. Route the local side through the cache. `loadVectorChunks` (:1868) and `persistVectorChunks` (:2454) each open a private `BNNSVectorDatabase` for a URL `VectorStoreRouter` may already hold open - the local store is opened three times per container per pass by three different instances of the same actor over the same files. Use `VectorStoreRouter.db(for:)` for the local URL. This is also a correctness point, not only cost: three live actors over one file, one of which calls `clear()` (BNNSVectorDatabase.swift:652, which deletes all three files), is the shape that produces "store exists but read as empty".

BOUNDARY: every one of 1-4 lands in `WorkspaceSyncService.swift`, which is a hard-boundary file. This cannot be implemented until the owner names that file in their approval. `ContentView.swift:237` is not boundary-protected but changing it alone would only mask channel 2(a), not fix it. `BNNSVectorDatabase.swift` is boundary-protected for its FORMAT; none of the above changes the on-disk format, but item 4 touches that file's callers only.

DIAGNOSTIC NOTE FOR THE OWNER: the instrumentation added in commit a840786 counts opens and writes in `mergeVectorStoresIfNeeded` (:1795) and logs "Vector merge pass starting/complete". That function is the one-time migration path and does not appear in this capture at all. The churn comes from `synchronizeVectorStore` (:2316), which has no such counter. Move the counter there and the next device log names the driver directly.
findings.expectedGain:
Countable and certain: on an idle boot with no real content change, 210 persists -> approximately 0, 432 loads -> approximately 4 (one per container via the router), and bytes written per boot drop from a measured floor of ~200 MB (likely ~370 MB, half of it queued as iCloud replacement uploads) to essentially nothing. Those numbers follow directly from the log arithmetic and the FPItem sizes and do not need a trace.

Wall-clock and hang impact: unknown without Instruments, and I am not going to guess. The heavy work is off the main actor (BNNSVectorDatabase is an actor; loadFromDisk and saveToDisk run on its executor), so the likely payoff is I/O bandwidth, dirty-page and memory pressure, iCloud upload queue depth and battery - not necessarily main-thread stall time. The 2.94s hang is logged one line BEFORE the first [BNNS] line in the capture, so nothing here attributes the hang to this churn.

Secondary effects that are more valuable than the milliseconds: the app currently deletes and rewrites every library's entire vector index roughly 21 times per boot for no content change, each time via clear() which removes all three files before rewriting them. That is a narrow window where a synced index does not exist on disk, repeated ~200 times a session, in the subsystem whose past failures (documented in the comments at :2380-2400) were exactly "index read as empty, user told to re-import".
findings.risk:
High-consequence file. WorkspaceSyncService is where a wrong guard has already destroyed indexes - its own comments at :2380-2400 and :1145-1160 record a pass that deleted another device's store and told the user to re-import documents that were never lost. Specific risks:

1. The no-op short-circuit must compare against what the DESTINATION actually holds, not against the pre-merge in-memory list. Compare `resolvedChunks` to `localChunks` for the local skip and to `sharedChunks` for the shared skip, separately - a single combined digest would skip a write that one root genuinely needs and leave the two roots permanently divergent, silently.

2. Suppressing metadata-query updates risks dropping a real remote change that lands during a pass. The safe form is path-scoped suppression of only the files this pass wrote, plus one re-check after the pass settles - never a blanket mute and never a plain time window.

3. Fixing the aux-file ping-pong changes which side wins a transcript/chat-history conflict. Comparing bytes before copying is behaviour-neutral when they are equal, which is the only case being changed; do not also "improve" the mtime tiebreak in the same edit.

4. Item 4 (routing the local store through VectorStoreRouter) changes actor identity and therefore ordering between sync and live retrieval. It is the most valuable change for correctness and the most likely to surface a latent race. It should be a separate commit from items 1-3.

5. Verification is weak here by the repo's own record: there are no end-to-end tests over sync, and the unit suite covers none of this. The only trustworthy check is another device capture counting `[BNNS] Loaded` / `Persisted` lines on an idle boot, before and after, with the same libraries present. Do not accept a simulator run as proof - the iCloud ubiquity container is what drives the loop.

Inside it: :2340 `loadVectorChunks(local)`, :2368 `loadVectorChunks(shared)`, :2445 `persistVectorChunks(-> localVectorURL)`, :2446 `persistVectorChunks(-> sharedVectorURL)`. `loadVectorChunks` constructs a BNNSVectorDatabase at :1876 and `persistVectorChunks` at :2461; `init` spawns `loadFromDisk` at BNNSVectorDatabase.swift:96, which emits `[BNNS] Loaded` at :207. Zero exceptions.

The capture contains 22 full passes: 17 over 5 containers (26 / 182 / 182 / 182 / 1451) and 5 over 4 containers after one 182-chunk store empties, plus 12 stray single loads. That gives loads 26:4*22=88(+3 stray)=91, 182:4*(3*17+2*5)=244(+6)=250, 1451:4*22=88, plus 3 `L0` = 432 exactly; persists 44 / 122 / 44 = 210 exactly. verdict.correction:
Nine corrections. None overturns the mechanism; several change what to do about it.

1. PASS COUNT AND RESIDUAL. It is 22 passes, not "~21", and the residual is 12 stray loads, not 3. The claim reached 429 by adding the per-store totals, which does not test the 4-per-pass model. The model does hold, with the decomposition in my reason field. Strays: L182 at Startup.txt:720, 805, 837, 896, 982, 1131; L26 at 901, 978, 1130; L0 at 891, 977, 1129. Note 1132 is the first load of the next pass, not a stray, so the cited example range "1129-1132" is off by one.

2. CHANNEL 2(b) IS REFUTED. The claim's premise is "coordinatedCopyItem removes and re-copies the destination and therefore always leaves the DESTINATION newer than the source", with the roles flipping each pass. `FileManager.copyItem` preserves the source's modification date. I tested it on this machine (Darwin 27, APFS): source backdated 1000 s, destination removed then copied, result `dst newer than src? false` with identical timestamps. `modificationDate(for:)` (:2824) reads `.contentModificationDateKey`, so the flip never happens. The capture corroborates: across all eight FPItem blocks the `c{54}` and `t{45}` json items keep pre-session mtimes (1786333518, 1786737182, 1786758672, 1786779123, 1786816766, 1786936114...) while the vector artifacts get five fresh ones - exactly the split you expect between `Data.write(.atomic)` and `copyItem`. The real defect at :2470 is different and still worth fixing: with equal mtimes `max(by:)` keeps the first maximal element, which is a local candidate, so :2515 re-copies the shared aux file every pass with no equality check at all. That burns I/O and generates FileProvider replacements, but it does not change the content date and therefore does not feed `workspaceSignature`. Fix 2(b) is worth doing for the I/O; its stated justification is wrong, and closing it will not slow the loop.

3. COST ARITHMETIC. The 1451-chunk `_meta.json` is measured in the log at 2.8 MB (Startup.txt:147, :305, :812), not "extrapolated at 2.9 KB/chunk to ~4.2 MB". Corrected per destination per pass: 26-store 99 KB + three 182-stores at 812 KB + 1451-store 5,126 KB = 7.5 MB; two destinations = 15.0 MB per pass; 17 five-container passes plus 5 four-container passes = ~320 MB written per session, ~160 MB of it into the ubiquity container. The claim's "measured floor ~9 MB per pass / ~200 MB per boot" understates by about 40 percent; its "likely ~370 MB" slightly overstates. The conclusion survives, the derivation should be replaced with the measured figure.

4. NOT A LIBRARY DELETION. Startup.txt:878-887 is a DOCUMENT deletion: `Deleted 182 chunks for document 85D0FC77-6D6A-4234-854E-36D22CFF33A4`, `Removed document: ...Yagishita...-3.pdf`, then `Loaded 0 chunks` at :891. The container survives with zero chunks, so its store no longer exists and it contributes no BNNS lines. Same arithmetic, wrong description.

5. DEAD CODE - stronger than the diagnostic note. `mergeVectorStoresIfNeeded` (:1795) is not merely "the migration path that did not run in this capture". Its only caller is `migrateCanonicalWorkspaceIfNeeded` (:1557), and a repo-wide grep finds zero call sites for that function. It is unreachable private code. The instrumentation added in the working tree - the `storeOpens`/`storeWrites` counters and the "Vector merge pass starting/complete" logs - can never fire on any device. Say that plainly to the owner rather than "move the counter".

6. THE HOT COST IS PROBABLY THE JSON DECODE, NOT THE MMAP COPY. The claim highlights `getEmbeddings(forIndices:)` (:750). But `loadFromDisk` decodes the whole `_meta.json` on every construction (BNNSVectorDatabase.swift:159-160), which for the 1451 store is 2.8 MB of JSON decoded 88 times per session; `allChunks()` then returns that array by value and `loadVectorChunks` builds a third copy at WorkspaceSyncService.swift:1881-1890. The heap copy the claim names is real but is likely the smaller of the three. Ranking them needs Instruments: needsInstruments.

7. FIX 1 HAS TWO DEFECTS. (a) `localChunks` and `sharedChunks` are concatenations over all `sourceContainerIDs` (:2339, :2367) that have then been rewritten by `applyingDocumentAliases` (:2344, :2374). They are not a digest of what sits at `localVectorURL` or `sharedVectorURL`. The proposed skip is only sound when `sourceContainerIDs == {container.id}` and no alias applied; otherwise it can skip a write the canonical destination needs. (b) A digest of "count + ordered chunk ids" cannot see an embedding change under unchanged ids - which is precisely the v5.0 re-embed case. Ship that guard and a model swap silently stops propagating vectors across devices. The digest must include something derived from the vectors (the norms array is already in hand and is cheap).

8. FIX 3 IS THE STRONGEST ITEM AND IS UNDERSOLD. All four `coordinatedMergeData` transforms already set `encoder.outputFormatting = [.prettyPrinted, .sortedKeys]`, so byte-identical output for identical content is actually achievable - the guard will fire, not just exist. Two caller notes: the guard must also skip the `.localWorkspaceDidChange` post at :3472, which sits outside the coordination block and would otherwise keep feeding the 2-second debounced reconfigure at :295; and `coordinatedMergeData` has an external caller at RAGService.swift:3730, which the change also affects (benignly, and in the same direction).

9. FIX 4 IS NARROWER AND RISKIER THAN DESCRIBED. `VectorStoreRouter.db(for:)` builds its URL from `AppSupportPaths.vectorsFileURL` -> `baseDirectory()`, which equals `applicationSupportRoot()` only when no override is set; under the benchmark/test base-directory override the router and the sync already point at different files, so routing through the router changes behavior there. `db(for:)` is also keyed by `KnowledgeContainer`, so it can cover only the canonical local URL, not the per-`sourceContainerID` opens at :2341. And sharing one actor does not remove the empty-store window: `clear()`, `storeBatch`, `persist()` are three separate awaits on that actor, so a query can still interleave and observe an empty index - arguably more visibly once the cached instance is the one being cleared. Keep the item, drop the "this is also a correctness fix" framing.

Boundary statement is correct: items 1-4 all land in WorkspaceSyncService.swift, which needs the owner to name that file. Minor citation nits: `isWorkspaceMetadataItemRelevant` is declared at :3280 (:3292 is the `vector_database_` filter line, which is what the claim actually means); `Self.isSyncWriteInProgress` is set at :356 in the same function the claim cites for the loop, and the flag does exist and does guard the four `coordinated*` helpers (:3420, :3471, :3499, :3536) and BNNSVectorDatabase :324 and :668 - it simply never reaches `handleMetadataQueryResults`, which is what the claim says.

Remaining uncertainty, stated plainly: channel (a) is proven as code but not observed closing in the capture. No FPItem in the log is identifiable as the shared containers.json or documents_metadata.json, and the log carries no timestamps, so the ordering of "pass writes shared json" -> "metadata query fires" -> "next pass" is inference from the event budget, not measurement. Confirming it needs either a device log with the metadata-query notification instrumented or an Instruments file-activity trace: needsInstruments.

findings.cause:
The launch hang is structural, not a single slow call: essentially the app's entire service graph is built synchronously on the main thread inside `ContentView.init`, and the MainActor continuations it schedules then chain into synchronous iCloud/FileProvider calls before the run loop is ever released. I can name every main-thread item in that window with a line number; I cannot attribute the 2.94s across them from this log, which has no timestamps.

What is on the main thread, in order:

1. `ContentView.init` (ContentView.swift:37-58) runs during the first body evaluation of `WindowGroup`, before first frame. It constructs nine services eagerly. Inside that:
   - `EmbeddingService.swift:53` has `provider: EmbeddingProvider = CoreMLSentenceEmbeddingProvider()` as an eager default argument, and that initializer calls `setup()`, which does a synchronous `MLModel(contentsOf:)` at CoreMLSentenceEmbeddingProvider.swift:165. Startup.txt:2 confirms it completes during launch. Nothing on the first frame embeds anything.
   - `ContainerService.swift:229` does an `NSFileCoordinator` read of containers.json on the main actor.
   - `RAGService.swift:1648` calls `loadDocumentsFromDisk()` synchronously, which at RAGService.swift:3654 does a second `NSFileCoordinator` read plus a `JSONDecoder` pass over documents_metadata.json on the main thread (10 docs / 2484 chunks, Startup.txt:15).

Moderate, and concentrated in the ordering changes rather than the lazy-load change.

- Item 4 touches WorkspaceSyncService.swift, which is a hard-boundary file. findings.cause:
The observation-churn defect that the capture actually measures is not @Published invalidating view bodies — it is SwiftUI observation hooks fanning out into unbounded fire-and-forget vector-store reload Tasks.

`RAGService.reloadWorkspaceData()` (RAGService.swift:3675) opens with `vectorRouter.clearAll()` (:3676). Despite the name, `VectorStoreRouter.clearAll()` (VectorStoreRouter.swift:160-168) evicts nothing: it keeps every cached store and spawns an un-awaited `Task { try? await db.reload() }` per store, with no dedupe and no in-flight guard. Each `reload()` is exactly one `[BNNS] Loaded` line (BNNSVectorDatabase.swift:460-467 -> :143 -> :207). Because `BNNSVectorDatabase` is an `actor` (:50), K concurrent reload Tasks on one store do not race — they serialize into K full mmap+decode passes.

`reloadWorkspaceData()` has 10 call sites. Four are SwiftUI reactive hooks that fire on lifecycle or publisher events rather than user intent:
- ContentView.swift:229 `.onChange(of: scenePhase)` -> :353 `.active` -> :356 `refreshSharedWorkspaceIfNeeded` -> :402 `reloadWorkspaceData()`. This branch logs nothing. Only `.inactive` logs (:372), so every `Scene became inactive` line in the capture is the visible half of an inactive->active round trip whose return leg silently reloads.
- ContentView.swift:232 `.onChange(of: containerService.containers.map {...})`
- ContentView.swift:237 `.onChange(of: workspaceSyncService.observedWorkspaceChangeCount)`
- DocumentLibraryView.swift:1309 `.onChange(of: workspaceSyncService.observedWorkspaceChangeCount)` -> :1338-1339

The last two observe the same counter, bumped by the iCloud NSMetadataQuery observer at WorkspaceSyncService.swift:3273 (registered :3218-3228). One bump therefore runs two independent full reloads. Their re-entrancy guards cannot suppress each other: `isRefreshingSharedWorkspace` is local @State inside DocumentLibraryView, and ContentView's `refreshSharedWorkspaceIfNeeded` (:381) has no guard at all. Fan-out is multiplicative: (handlers that fired) x (cached stores) reload Tasks per event.

Separately, the publisher surface itself is oversubscribed but NOT shown to cost anything in this capture. RAGService declares 24 @Published (RAGService.swift:1327-1381) and is subscribed whole by 32 property wrappers across 23 view files: 9 `@EnvironmentObject var ragService` declarations (4 files: VisualizationsView x4, AdaptiveVisualizationsView x3, Embedding3DView, DatabaseDashboardView), 22 `@ObservedObject`, and 1 `@StateObject` at the app root (ContentView.swift:16). Observation framework adoption is effectively zero: 26 ObservableObject conformances against exactly one `@Observable` type (HardwareTelemetryState.swift:122).

- Per-token @Published writes. Chat streaming holds text in ChatScreen's local `@State streamingText`/`streamingBuffer` (ChatScreen.swift:203-205) behind a pump task; RAGService's live counters update per agentic step, not per token (:8147-8167).

verdict.reason:
The claim's code reading is almost entirely accurate, but its central causal mechanism is contradicted by the capture it cites. I opened every line and then tested the mechanism against the log shape.

WHAT VERIFIED CLEANLY
- VectorStoreRouter.swift:160-168 — `clearAll()` really does not clear. It iterates `stores` and fires `Task { try? await db.reload() }` un-awaited, no dedupe, no in-flight guard. Exactly as described.
- RAGService.swift:3675/:3676 — `reloadWorkspaceData()` opens with `vectorRouter.clearAll()`. 10 call sites confirmed by grep.
- BNNSVectorDatabase.swift:50 `actor`; :460-467 `reload()` awaits then unconditionally re-runs `loadFromDisk`; :143 `loadFromDisk`; :207 the single `[BNNS] Loaded` line. Also confirmed (claim did not note it): `init` at :90-100 spawns `loadTask` too, so every construction emits one `Loaded`.
- ContentView.swift:16, :229, :232, :237, :353, :356, :372, :381, :402 — all as cited. `.active` logs nothing while `.inactive` logs at :372. Confirmed.
- DocumentLibraryView.swift:1309 — a second, independent `.onChange` on the same `observedWorkspaceChangeCount`. Confirmed, and its `isRefreshingSharedWorkspace` (:64) is local `@State`, so it cannot see ContentView's pass.
- WorkspaceSyncService.swift:3273 `observedWorkspaceChangeCount += 1`, observer registered :3218-3228 on `.NSMetadataQueryDidUpdate`. Confirmed.
- Publisher-surface facts: 24 `@Published` at RAGService.swift:1327-1381; zero `objectWillChange` anywhere in the repo; all 7 named properties have zero readers outside RAGService.swift; `processingStatus` written at RAGService.swift:4914 on every ingestion tick with no view reader (OnboardingChecklistView.swift:51 is that view's own `@State`); DocumentCard.swift:12 `@ObservedObject` reading only `syncMode(for:)` (RAGService.swift:3839-3842), which touches `containerService.containers`, not a RAGService `@Published`; ModelResolutionService.swift:111 and :119 both re-publish RAGService changes through `.receive(on: RunLoop.main)`; HardwareTelemetryState.swift:122 is the only `@Observable`. All confirmed.
- The refusal to attribute the 2.94s hang is correct. Hang at Startup.txt:47, first load at :48.

WHY THE MECHANISM FAILS
`reload()` produces a bare `[BNNS] Loaded`. It never calls `storeBatch` and never dirties the store, so it can never produce `[BNNS] Batch buffered` (BNNSVectorDatabase.swift:446) or `[BNNS] Persisted` (:456, gated by `guard isDirty || !pendingEmbeddings.isEmpty` at :453).

The capture holds 432 `Loaded`, 210 `Batch buffered`, 210 `Persisted`. Extracting the BNNS event sequence and doing a run-length analysis of consecutive `Loaded` lines gives: 105 runs of exactly 1, 100 runs of exactly 3, and only five anomalous runs (one 4, one 5, three 6s). Every run terminates in `Batch buffered` + `Persisted`. The repeating unit across the entire 1213-line file is:

  Loaded, Loaded, Loaded, Batch buffered, Persisted, Loaded, Batch buffered, Persisted

That is a construct-clear-storeBatch-persist shape, not a reload shape. `mergeVectorStoresIfNeeded` (WorkspaceSyncService.swift:1795) opens three databases per container — two in `loadVectorChunks` (:1876) and one for the merge (:1857) — then `clear()`, `storeBatch` (:1862), `persist()`. That is exactly `[L L L B P]`. `persistVectorChunks` (:2461) is exactly `[L B P]`. These constructions bypass `VectorStoreRouter` entirely, so nothing is cached across passes.

Un-awaited `Task`s from `clearAll()` would land at arbitrary points and smear that distribution into runs of 2, 4, 5, 7. They do not. At most 27 of 432 loads (6%) sit outside the clean 3/1 model, and the genuinely isolated orphan `Loaded` lines with no adjacent write — Startup.txt:805, :837, :891, :896, :901 — number about five. Those five are the plausible `clearAll()` contribution: roughly 1% of the measured churn, and all on the 182-chunk store, consistent with `VectorStoreRouter.stores` typically holding only the active container.

So fix item 3, "make `clearAll()` idempotent," addresses about 1% of the loads and 0% of the writes. It is the wrong target.

Burst segmentation adds a second problem for the claim. Bursts cluster at exactly 20 and 40 loads: 20, 20, 20, 40, 20, 40, 40, 20, 40, 20, 41, 21, 35, 16, 19, 16. One full sync pass over {26 x1, 182 x3, 1451 x1} is 20 loads. Under the claim's model the fan-out is (handlers) x (cached stores) with no coalescing, which predicts a continuous spread, not a hard 1x/2x quantization.

WHAT THE CLAIM MISSED IN THE CODE
- `reconfigureIfNeeded` (WorkspaceSyncService.swift:340-372) already has an in-flight guard: `isReconfigureInProgress` plus a `needsReconfigurePass` flag driving `repeat { } while`. N overlapping callers collapse to at most 2 passes. That is precisely the 20-vs-40 quantization in the log, and it means the duplicate-observer thesis is right about the trigger while being wrong about where the cost multiplies.
- `observedWorkspaceChangeCount` does not bump on every FileProvider event. WorkspaceSyncService.swift:3266 guards on a workspace signature diff first, so the 112 permission errors are not evidence of 112 bumps.
- ContentView.swift:382 runs `await workspaceSyncService.reconfigureIfNeeded()` BEFORE the cheap-exit guard at :383. The expensive sync pass — the thing that actually produces the 432 loads and 210 writes — is completely outside the guard the claim proposes tightening. DocumentLibraryView.swift:1034 does guard before its `reconfigureIfNeeded()` at :1043.
- `restorePersistedIngestionQueueIfNeeded` has three call sites (:953, :1668, :3684), not one, so the 8 `Dropping` groups are ~7 `reloadWorkspaceData()` calls plus the startup pass. The "~8" estimate survives; the "one fingerprint" reasoning does not.

FIX-SAFETY PROBLEM
Deleting DocumentLibraryView.swift:1309-1313 is not behaviour-neutral. That handler reaches `performSharedWorkspaceRefresh` (:1032), whose not-shared branch calls `presentSharedSyncReviewIfNeeded()` (:1046). ContentView's `refreshSharedWorkspaceIfNeeded` has no equivalent, so the shared-sync conflict review would stop being offered on a metadata bump (it would survive only via `onAppear` -> `autoRefreshSharedWorkspaceIfNeeded` at :1012). The two handlers also do different work: ContentView's invalidates visualization, cluster, suggested-question and Spotlight caches for removed containers (:394-400); the library's does not.

CITATION ERRORS
DocumentLibraryView's reload pair is at :1063-1064 (inside `performSharedWorkspaceRefresh`, reached via `handleObservedSharedWorkspaceChange` at :1026), not :1338-1339 — :1338 is inside `ingestionQueueOverlay`. `ContainerService` lives at Services/Infrastructure/Integration/ContainerService.swift; `containers = loaded` is :65 not :64, `loadContainers` is :225 not :230, and `updateStats`'s `guard hasChanges` is :211 not :257. `WindowGroup` is OpenIntelligenceApp.swift:41-45, not :40-43. Counts: 21 `@ObservedObject` not 22 (31 wrappers total, not 32, across 23 files as claimed); 24 `ObservableObject` conformances, not 26. And the brief's own premise that WorkspaceSyncService carries three log statements is now stale: commit a840786 ("make the sync service's vector-store work visible in a trace", 2026-08-18, after the capture) added `Log.debug` instrumentation at exactly the three bypassing construction sites (:1871, :2456) plus a merge-pass counter (:1820, :1825). The file now has 16. Its own comment at :1805-1816 already names `mergeVectorStoresIfNeeded` as the source of the 432/210 numbers.

NOT RE-VERIFIABLE FROM SOURCE
The claim's own honesty about item 4 is right and I did nothing to change it. `needsInstruments`: whether 31 whole-object subscriptions and 7 zero-reader publishers cost frame time is not answerable by reading code, and neither is whether the actor-serialized mmap+decode passes contend with the main thread. The load/write counts are countable; the cost per load is not, and nothing in the capture times a single load.
verdict.correction:
Right diagnosis, wrong organ. Keep the trigger analysis; discard `clearAll()` as the cost centre.

MEASURED CAUSE
Every burst is `WorkspaceSyncService`'s vector-store synchronization, not `VectorStoreRouter.clearAll()`. `mergeVectorStoresIfNeeded` (WorkspaceSyncService.swift:1795) constructs three `BNNSVectorDatabase` instances per candidate container per pass — `loadVectorChunks` twice (:1876) and the merge target once (:1857) — then clears, re-buffers and re-persists every chunk (:1862). `persistVectorChunks` (:2461) adds a fourth construct-and-write. All four bypass `VectorStoreRouter`, the only thing that caches stores, and `BNNSVectorDatabase.init` (:90-100) reads from disk. One pass over this user's containers is 20 `[BNNS] Loaded` and 10 `[BNNS] Persisted`; the capture holds 432 and 210, i.e. roughly 21 passes in one boot plus tab navigation. The work is not merely redundant reads — it rewrites 26, 182 and 1451 chunks to disk 105 times, in an app whose files are also being uploaded by iCloud.

WHAT THE CLAIM GOT RIGHT AND SHOULD KEEP
The reactive-trigger fan-out is real and is what schedules those passes. Two independent handlers watch `observedWorkspaceChangeCount` (ContentView.swift:237, DocumentLibraryView.swift:1309) and their guards cannot see each other. Burst sizes quantize at exactly 20 and 40 loads — one pass and two — which is what `reconfigureIfNeeded`'s `isReconfigureInProgress` + `needsReconfigurePass` loop (WorkspaceSyncService.swift:350-372) produces when one versus two callers arrive. That is quantitative support for the duplicate-observer thesis. Treat it as a strong inference, not proof; commit a840786's new merge-pass counters at :1820 and :1825 will settle it on the next capture.

REVISED FIX ORDER
1. Move the expensive call inside the guard. ContentView.swift:382 awaits `reconfigureIfNeeded()` before the cheap-exit guard at :383, so the guard protects only `reloadWorkspaceData()`. Reorder so a no-op refresh cannot trigger a full sync pass. This is a small, local change and is where the measured cost enters on the scene-phase path.
2. Make the sync pass content-addressed. Inside `mergeVectorStoresIfNeeded`, skip a container when the local and shared vector artifacts' mtime and size are unchanged since the last pass. Today the loop rewrites identical data every time. This is the single highest-value change and it is independent of how many handlers fire.
3. Give the sync service a store cache, or route these three constructions through `VectorStoreRouter`. Note the constraint: WorkspaceSyncService.swift is a hard-boundary file and cannot be edited without the owner naming it. Items 1 and 2 both touch it as well (item 1 only reorders ContentView, which is not boundary-protected; item 2 is inside the boundary file). Say so before proposing them as work.
4. Deduplicate the counter observers — but audit the delta first. Removing DocumentLibraryView.swift:1309-1313 drops the only path that reaches `presentSharedSyncReviewIfNeeded()` (:1046) on a metadata bump, and ContentView's handler additionally invalidates visualization/cluster/suggested-question/Spotlight caches (:394-400). Merge the two behaviours into one entry point rather than deleting one.
5. Do not bother making `clearAll()` idempotent for performance. It accounts for roughly five of 432 loads in this capture (the orphan `Loaded` lines at Startup.txt:805, :837, :891, :896, :901) and zero writes. Renaming it is still worth doing on clarity grounds — it does not clear — but bill that as hygiene, not perf.
6. Item 4 of the original (dropping `@Published` from zero-reader properties, `let` instead of `@ObservedObject` in the 7 non-reading views) stands exactly as the claim framed it, including the caveat: unknown without Instruments. `needsInstruments` — run the SwiftUI template's View Body and View Properties lanes during ingestion and during a large-library scroll before spending effort.

STILL UNEXPLAINED
Why the 182-chunk store is processed three times per pass while the 26 and 1451 stores are processed once. That ratio (250/91/88 loads) is stable across every burst and is not explained by anything I read. The new instrumentation at :1820/:1825 prints candidate count and store opens per pass and should answer it in one capture.

The 2.94s hang remains unattributed, as the claim correctly said. It is logged at Startup.txt:47, before the first load at :48, and nothing here touches it.

verdict.reason:
The claim splits into a mechanism half and an attribution half. The mechanism half verifies almost perfectly. The attribution half — which is the dimension's actual thesis, "what each tab costs on switch" — is contradicted by the claim's own capture.

WHAT VERIFIED (every cited line opened and read)

Trigger chain, confirmed unconditional. DocumentLibraryView.swift:1076 body -> :1080 libraryAlertView -> :1182 librarySheetView -> :1265 libraryChromeView -> :1294, with .onAppear at :1304 calling autoRefreshSharedWorkspaceIfNeeded (:1012) and the unthrottled .onChange at :1309 calling handleObservedSharedWorkspaceChange (:1026). Both real, both reachable. workspaceSyncService is @EnvironmentObject (:16), so :1309 is live, not dead.

Throttle, confirmed honest. :1016-1020 reads workspaceSyncService.lastSyncAttemptAt with a 15s floor; recordSyncAttempt (WorkspaceSyncService.swift:886-890) is called at :428, before synchronizeConfiguredLibraries at :487/:502/:541/:554/:624. Stamped before the work, as claimed.

Cost arithmetic, confirmed line-for-line. synchronizeVectorStore (:2316) does loadVectorChunks twice (each constructing a BNNSVectorDatabase at :1876) then persistVectorChunks twice (:2445-2446, construction at :2461, then clear + storeBatch + persist). That predicts L,L,L,P,L,P per library. I dumped the actual sequence of all 432 BNNS lines: every burst is exactly L26 L26 L26 P26 L26 P26, then three identical 182 blocks, then 1451 — five libraries, 4 opens and 2 rewrites each. The code predicts the log exactly. This is the strongest part of the claim and it holds.

Dead-code ruling, confirmed and independently corroborated. migrateCanonicalWorkspaceIfNeeded (WorkspaceSyncService.swift:1557) has zero call sites repo-wide, so mergeVectorStoresIfNeeded (:1795) is unreachable and the instrumentation comment at :1806-1815 does mis-attribute the 432 loads. Second, independent proof the claim missed: that loop does 3 opens + 1 write per container (:1846-1847, :1856), which would print L,L,L,P — the log prints L,L,L,P,L,P. The shape alone discriminates.

Off-main ruling, confirmed. BNNSVectorDatabase is an actor (:50); init (:90) defers the read into loadTask = Task { await self.loadFromDisk(url:) } (:96-98). The MainActor.run wrappers at :1876 and :2461 enclose only three stored-property assignments plus a Task creation.

Atlas and Database, confirmed. AdaptiveVisualizationsView.swift:205 bare .task and :208 .task(id:) both call refreshAnalysis (:818). LibraryVisualizationEngine.swift:293 is @MainActor with no nonisolated, Task.detached or DispatchQueue in the file; profileCache is written at :381 and read nowhere (:304 decl, :332 and :341 evict); analyzeTopics (:447) loops every chunk tokenizing content with no suspension point, so it holds the main actor. DatabaseDashboardView.swift:180 .task has no freshness guard, and :191 seeding databaseScope trips :188 for an extra loadStatistics on first entry; 6 FTS5 queries confirmed (2 in Phase 1, 4 in Phase 2). Zero "[DatabaseDash]" lines in 1213 capture lines, so that tab was never opened. Chat and Settings are cheap as described: ChatScreen.swift:600's .task(id:) short-circuits on lastLoadedChatContainerId / lastProcessedContainerId at :622-624, and RAGService.swift:17309 really does cache checkDeviceCapabilities.

WHAT REFUTES IT

1. The tab is a constant, so it cannot explain the variance. Startup.txt contains exactly one [TabBar] line, at :90. The app sits on Documents for lines 90-1213 — 92% of the capture. The claim asserts "on any other tab one iCloud change costs one pass; on Documents it costs two" and offers the 20/10 vs 40/20 split as proof. But there is no "other tab" period in the capture to compare against.

2. The 40/20 bursts track scene phase, not the tab. Segmenting all 432 BNNS lines (gap > 3) gives 22 bursts. Exactly five are 40/20, starting at lines 212, 366, 456, 587, 720. Each is immediately preceded by "[App] Scene became inactive" at lines 210, 364, 452, 580, 713 — a 5-for-5 match within 2 to 7 lines. No 20/10 burst is preceded by a scene line. The claim cites three of these five (212, 456, 587) as its evidence for tab-dependence; all three follow a scene-phase transition.

3. Four single passes happen while on the Documents tab. Bursts at 166, 322, 540 and 671 are 20/10 and all occur after the tab switch, with the Documents tab on screen. If :1309 doubled every iCloud change on that tab, those would be 40/20. They are not. The doubling is not tab-conditioned.

4. The mechanism that does fit. ContentView.swift:353-357: the .active branch of handleScenePhaseChange calls refreshSharedWorkspaceIfNeeded(forceReload: workspaceSyncService.isUsingSharedWorkspace) on every return to active. The .inactive branch (:366-372) only checkpoints. Combined with reconfigureIfNeeded's coalescing (WorkspaceSyncService.swift:350-353 sets needsReconfigurePass when a second caller arrives mid-flight, and the repeat loop at :364-368 then runs one more pass), an inactive-to-active round trip plus the concurrent metadata trigger yields exactly two sequential passes. That is a scene-phase amplifier. [evidence_level: log correlation 5/5 plus a read code path, confidence: medium-high — the .active transition is not itself logged, so this needs one instrumented build to close.]

5. Burst 1 is not attributable to the tab switch. Burst 0 (lines 48-87) has the identical shape — 20/10 over the same five stores in the same order — and it ran at launch on the Chat tab, before line 90. So a whole-workspace rewrite is not something entering Documents uniquely causes. And burst 0 ran recordSyncAttempt, which stamps lastSyncAttemptAt before the work, so the :1016-1020 throttle should have rejected an onAppear arriving within 15s. The capture has no timestamps (I checked the line format), so whether 15s elapsed between line 87 and line 90 is unknowable. Burst 1 is temporally adjacent to the tab switch and nothing more. Burst 2 (166-205) is an identical pass with no tab switch at all.

6. Frequency is shown; cost is not, for the part that matters. The claim concedes this itself, correctly. Nothing in the confirmed path blocks the main thread. The one main-actor CPU cost identified — buildProfile/analyzeTopics over 1451 chunks — is in a tab that was never opened in this capture, so its cost is unmeasured. needsInstruments.

FIX REVIEW

Step 1 (delete the bare .task at :205) is correct, safe, and understated: analysisTask?.cancel() at :356 does not stop the running buildProfile, because neither buildProfile (:390) nor analyzeTopics (:447) checks Task.isCancelled — the only check is at :375, after buildProfile returns. So the duplicate costs a full duplicate profile build, not just a duplicate hydration.

Step 2 (read profileCache) is directionally right but the eviction story is weaker than stated. Per-container eviction fires only from ContentView.swift:395 (containers removed by a workspace reload), LibraryDeletion.swift:108, and DocumentLibraryView.swift:1640. The no-argument LibraryVisualizationEngine.invalidateCache() at :329 has zero call sites repo-wide — dead. So a content change that leaves chunkCount and documentCount unchanged would serve a stale profile under the proposed guard.

Step 3 is where the claimed gain fails. The stated falsifiable prediction — "the 40-load / 20-persist bursts should become 20 / 10" — will almost certainly not happen, because those bursts follow scene-phase transitions. Removing :1309 does remove a genuine unthrottled duplicate trigger and is probably still worth doing, but predict no change to the 40/20 bursts. The presentSharedSyncReviewIfNeeded caveat is also over-cautious: it sits inside performSharedWorkspaceRefresh at :1046 and stays reachable from the :1304 onAppear path and the manual refresh, so deleting :1309 does not orphan it.

Step 4 is sound and low-risk.

Step 5 correctly flags WorkspaceSyncService.swift as a hard-boundary file needing the owner to name it. One overstatement: "2 opens per library and 0 writes instead of 4 and 2" is not reachable. The fail-closed path at :2354-2364 and the empty-resolution branch both require actually loading both stores, so the comparison must happen after the two loads. The saving is the 2 writes and the 2 opens inside persistVectorChunks — 2 opens and 0 writes is the floor only if you also skip both persists, which is what is being proposed, so the arithmetic works out, but it cannot go below the 2 diagnostic loads.

ONE POINT IN THE CLAIM'S FAVOUR IT DID NOT MAKE. isWorkspaceMetadataItemRelevant (WorkspaceSyncService.swift:3292-3294) explicitly excludes files prefixed "vector_database_", so the shared-store rewrites do not themselves retrigger the metadata observer. The most obvious self-feeding loop is ruled out by that filter.

MINOR CITATION ERRORS. ChatScreen.swift:864 is .onAppear, not the refreshDynamicQuestions guard — that guard is at :655. ContentView.swift:396 is ClusterLabelService; the LibraryVisualizationEngine invalidation is at :395. The "same tails" pair in ContentView is :391 and :402, not :401-402. None of these change the argument.

VERDICT. Confirm the mechanism, reject the dimension. The claim establishes what a sync pass costs and why, in verifiable detail. It does not establish that entering the Documents tab is what pays it, and its stated amplifier is refuted by its own capture.

findings.cause:
`ContentView.init()` builds the entire service graph synchronously on the main thread before SwiftUI ever evaluates `body`, and three of those constructors do real blocking work inline: a 43 MB CoreML model load targeted at the ANE, and two `NSFileCoordinator`-coordinated file reads each followed by a full `JSONDecoder` decode.

The log proves the ordering rather than inferring it. `Startup.txt:1` is emitted by `StoreKitTestHarness.swift:9`, reached only from `ContentView.swift:34`. `Startup.txt:2` is `CoreMLSentenceEmbeddingProvider.swift:169`, i.e. the line immediately after `MLModel(contentsOf:configuration:)` at `:168`. `Startup.txt:3` is `RAGService.swift:1571` and `Startup.txt:8` is `RAGService.swift:1639`. So log lines 1 through 8 are all inside one synchronous `ContentView.init()` call on the main thread, and `Hang detected: 2.94s (overlaps extended launch)` lands at `Startup.txt:47`, after them.

The chain: `ContentView.swift:38` constructs `ContainerService()`, whose `init` at `ContainerService.swift:21` calls `loadContainers()`, which does a coordinated read (`:229`) and decodes `[KnowledgeContainer]` (`:230`) on the main actor. `ContentView.swift:41` constructs `RAGService`, whose `init` at `RAGService.swift:1542` creates `EmbeddingService()`, whose default argument `CoreMLSentenceEmbeddingProvider()` (`EmbeddingService.swift:53`) runs `setup()` (`CoreMLSentenceEmbeddingProvider.swift:93`) and blocks on `MLModel(contentsOf:configuration:)` (`:168`) with `computeUnits = .cpuAndNeuralEngine` — the log's "ANE+CPU (efficiency mode)". The model is 43 MB (`OpenIntelligence/Resources/MLModels/EmbeddingModel.mlpackage`). The same `init` then calls `loadDocumentsFromDisk()` at `RAGService.swift:1654`, which runs the coordinated read and `[Document]` decode synchronously at `:3640` before handing the already-decoded result to a `Task { @MainActor }` — the hop is after the I/O, so it buys nothing.

`WorkspaceSyncService.coordinatedReadData` (`:3371`) and `coordinatedWriteData` (`:3397`) are both fully synchronous `NSFileCoordinator.coordinate` calls with no async variant, so every main-actor caller blocks the main thread for the coordination round-trip plus the read or atomic write.

The same primitives keep blocking the main actor after launch: `RAGService.savePersistedIngestionQueueState()` (`@MainActor`, `:1013`) encodes JSON and does a coordinated write at `:1038`, and `restorePersistedIngestionQueueIfNeeded()` (`@MainActor`, `:1045`) does a coordinated read at `:1055`. Take the blocking work out of `ContentView.init()`, smallest and highest-confidence change first.

1. Defer the CoreML load. In `CoreMLSentenceEmbeddingProvider`, stop calling `setup()` from `init` (`:93`). Get the recurring coordinated I/O off the main actor. `savePersistedIngestionQueueState` (`RAGService.swift:1013`) already has all it needs to encode on the main actor and then write from a `Task.detached` — that is exactly the pattern `ContainerService.saveContainers` (`:278-285`) and `TranscriptPersistenceService.saveTranscript` (`:58-66`) already use. Do the same for the read in `restorePersistedIngestionQueueIfNeeded` (`:1055`): read and decode in a `nonisolated` async helper, then apply on the main actor.

Better still, persist a small per-container index (id, name, updatedAt) so the sidebar never decodes message bodies.

Honestly: unknown without Instruments. What I can state from source is that a 43 MB CoreML load with ANE compute units, two `NSFileCoordinator` reads and two full JSON decodes all execute on the main thread inside the launch window and are all removable from it. What fraction of the measured 2.94s each accounts for is not derivable by reading code, and SwiftUI/CoreML launch guesses made this way are usually wrong.

Two things bound the estimate. The capture is a Debug build (`Startup.txt:1` is `#if DEBUG`-only, `StoreKitTestHarness.swift:8`), so the Release number is smaller than 2.94s to begin with. And the load target is an A18 Pro, where ANE model preparation is fast in absolute terms.

findings.risk:
No hard-boundary file needs editing as proposed. One caveat: if you would rather add async variants of the coordinated primitives than move each caller off the main actor, that means editing `coordinatedReadData`/`coordinatedWriteData` in `WorkspaceSyncService.swift` (`:3371`, `:3397`), which is on the hard-boundary list and needs the owner to name the file. A device where the resource is present but `MLModel(contentsOf:)` would fail now reports available at selection time and fails later, at first `embed`. `EmbeddingService.forProvider` (`:178-207`) would no longer fall through to NLEmbedding for that device. Handle it by having `ensureLoaded()` fall back on load failure and surface a clear error, and confirm the existing behaviour is actually reachable before assuming it matters.

- **Startup ordering.** Something at launch may already depend on the embedding provider being usable synchronously. `EmbeddingService.init` logs an availability warning at `:60`, and `RAGService.instantiateService` runs during the same init. findings.cause:
The chat transcript re-parses markdown from scratch inside a view body, with no memoization, and the surrounding view graph guarantees that body runs far more often than the content changes.

MECHANISM (three linked parts, all cited):

1. The parse is in the body. `MarkdownText.body` calls `MarkdownParser.parse(text)` as its first statement (MarkdownRenderer.swift:703). `parse` begins with `normalizeInlineMarkdown` (MarkdownRenderer.swift:70-171), which runs FOURTEEN separate `String.replacingOccurrences(of:with:options:.regularExpression)` passes over the entire message string (lines 78, 86, 94, 102, 109, 116, 123, 128, 136, 143, 148, 157, 162, 169). Eleven of the fourteen use ICU lookbehind (`(?<=\S)`, `(?<=[.!?:])`, `(?<=\|)`), the slowest construct in that engine. The block loop then runs a further regex per non-empty line (MarkdownRenderer.swift:223) and per numbered line (365, 369). Each resulting paragraph block is handed to `InlineMarkdownText`, whose body builds `AttributedString(markdown:)` — a second, full CommonMark parse — again inside the body (MarkdownRenderer.swift:456). The grounded-answer path adds a fifteenth whole-string regex before any of that (GroundedAnswerView.swift:31). Nothing anywhere in MarkdownRenderer.swift caches: `grep -i cache` over the file returns zero hits.

2. Every transcript row reaches it. `MessageBubbleV2` renders `MarkdownText(message.content, ...)` at MessageBubbleV2.swift:99, and its alternate branch `GroundedAnswerView` reaches the same code at GroundedAnswerView.swift:37. There is no third branch.

3. The body is re-run for every visible row on every list re-render, because SwiftUI cannot prove the rows are unchanged. `MessageListV2` mints six fresh closures per row inside the `ForEach` (MessageListV2.swift:84-89: `snapshot.role == .assistant ? { onRegenerate?(snapshot) } : nil` and five siblings), and `ChatScreen` mints six fresh closures for the list itself (ChatScreen.swift:2074-2103). SwiftUI's structural comparison of a non-Equatable view compares those fields as heap pointers, which differ on every construction, so the comparison fails and the body re-evaluates.

WHAT DRIVES THE RE-RENDER, AND HOW OFTEN:

PER-STATE-CHANGE, 12-25 Hz, during streaming — this is the expensive one. `streamingText` is `@State` on ChatScreen (ChatScreen.swift:203) and is appended by `pumpStreamingBuffer` at an 80 ms cadence, tightening to 40 ms under backlog (ChatScreen.swift:3054, 3061-3070, 3079), wrapped in `withAnimation(.linear(duration: 0.04))`. Each append re-evaluates `chatContentArea`, which re-constructs `MessageListV2` with fresh closures, which re-constructs every realized `MessageBubbleV2` with fresh closures. So 12-25 times per second, every already-finished message on screen is re-normalized through 14 lookbehind regex passes and re-parsed into AttributedString — not just the streaming bubble. The streaming bubble itself (MessageListV2.swift:232) additionally re-parses the whole accumulated answer each tick, which is O(length x ticks) in the answer length.

PER-ROW-APPEARANCE, during scroll. The `LazyVStack` (MessageListV2.swift:74) realizes a row as it enters view; that realization is the first `MarkdownText.body` call for that message, so the full 14-pass parse plus AttributedString lands inside a scroll frame. Long assistant answers pay proportionally to their length. Same shape for `DocumentLibraryView`'s `LazyVStack` (DocumentLibraryView.swift:202-203), though document cards contain no markdown.

PER-FRAME, potential, unverified. `BottomAnchorGeometry` publishes the anchor's `minY` as a preference on every scroll frame (MessageListV2.swift:120, 445-455), and `onPreferenceChange` writes `@State isPinnedToBottom` (MessageListV2.swift:150-155). If SwiftUI de-duplicates an equal `@State` write, the Bool only flips at the threshold and this costs nothing. If it does not, the entire list re-renders on every scroll frame, and via mechanism 3 that means the full markdown re-parse of every visible message at 120 Hz. I could not settle this from source and it is the single highest-leverage thing to check first.

findings.risk:
Moderate, concentrated in one place: MarkdownRenderer.swift is the rendering path for every answer the app produces, so a regression there is immediately visible to users on the primary screen.

Specific risks:
1. Rewriting the 14 `String.replacingOccurrences(of:options:.regularExpression)` calls as pre-compiled `NSRegularExpression` + `stringByReplacingMatches` changes the range/index semantics from String to NSString (UTF-16). Any answer containing emoji or non-BMP characters could shift a replacement boundary. This is the single most likely way to break it. Mitigate by keeping the `String`-level API and adding only the cache in the first pass, then doing the pattern hoist as a separate, separately-verified change. The cache alone captures most of the win.
2. The template semantics are load-bearing and already burned this repo once — GroundedAnswerView.swift:24-30 documents a shipped bug where `$$1` in an ICU template produced a dead `citation://$3` link on every citation tap. Any template touched here needs the same scrutiny.
3. Cache correctness: blocks depend only on `text`, so keying on text alone is sound, but keying the *view* rather than the blocks would be wrong (font, fontSize and foregroundColor vary by call site). Cache the blocks, not the view.
4. Unbounded growth. Use NSCache with an explicit countLimit; a long session streams a lot of distinct strings, one per tick, and a plain Dictionary would leak the entire transcript history.
5. Changing `MessageBubbleV2`'s callback signatures touches a view rendered in the app's main screen; a mis-wired callback silently disables Regenerate, Translate or Illustrate with no compile error if the closure shapes happen to match. Exercise all six actions on device.
6. `MarkdownParserTesting` (MarkdownRenderer.swift:52-59) is an existing DEBUG test seam for horizontal-rule detection — keep it working.
7. Adding a bounded cache is a behaviour change in memory pressure terms; the app already handles memory pressure in VectorStoreRouter, so the new cache should respond to the same signal rather than ignoring it.

Verification is awkward here and that is itself a risk: per repo memory there are no end-to-end tests covering these seams, `xcodebuild` must not be run from this session, and `VersionHistoryTests` makes USER_CHANGELOG.md a build input, so the owner should freeze docs before any verification run.
